abstract: Learning in strategy games (e.g. StarCraft, poker) requires the discovery of diverse policies. This is often achieved by iteratively training new policies against existing ones, growing a policy population that is robust to exploit. This iterative approach suffers from two issues in real-world games: a) under finite budget, approximate best-response operators at each iteration needs truncating, resulting in under-trained good-responses populating the population; b) repeated learning of basic skills at each iteration is wasteful and becomes intractable in the presence of increasingly strong opponents. In this work, we propose Neural Population Learning (NeuPL) as a solution to both issues. NeuPL offers convergence guarantees to a population of best-responses under mild assumptions. By representing a population of policies within a single conditional model, NeuPL enables transfer learning across policies. Empirically, we show the generality, improved performance and efficiency of NeuPL across several test domains. Most interestingly, we show that novel strategies become more accessible, not less, as the neural population expands.
text:
# NEUPL: NEURAL POPULATION LEARNING

Anonymous authors

Paper under double-blind review

# ABSTRACT

Learning in strategy games (e.g. StarCraft, poker) requires the discovery of diverse policies. This is often achieved by training new policies against existing ones, growing a population of policies that collectively become robust to exploit. Unfortunately, this approach suffers from two fundamental issues in real-world games: a) under finite compute budget, approximate best-response procedure often needs truncating, resulting in good-responses populating the policy population; b) in skill-based games, tabula rasa learning of best-responses is wasteful and quickly become computationally intractable, facing increasingly skillful opponents. In this work, we propose Neural Population Learning (NeuPL) as a solution to both issues. NeuPL offers convergence guarantees to a population of best-responses under mild conditions. By representing an entire population of policies within a single conditional model, NeuPL enables skill transfer across policies by construction. Empirically, we show the generality, improved performance and efficiency of NeuPL across several test domains<sup>1</sup>. Most interestingly, we show that novel strategies become more accessible, not less, as the neural population expands.

The need for learning not one, but a population of strategies is rooted in classical game theory. Consider the purely cyclical game of rock-paper-scissors, the performance of individual strategies is meaningless as improving against one entails losing to another. By contrast, performance can be meaningfully examined between populations. For instance, a population consisting of pure strategies  $\{\text{rock}, \text{paper}\}$  is said to do well against a singleton population of  $\{\text{scissors}\}$  because in the meta-game where both populations are known, a player picking strategies from the former can always beat a player choosing from the latter<sup>2</sup>. This observation underpins recent successes combining population learning and deep reinforcement learning (deep RL) in complex multi-agent domains (Jaderberg et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2021). Most impressively, Vinyals et al. (2019) explored the strategy game of StarCraft where exploiters to prioritize mixtures of opponents are introduced to a growing league of policies. The league counted close to a thousand sophisticated deep RL agents as the population collectively became robust to exploits.

Unfortunately, such empirical successes often come at considerable costs. Population learning algorithms with theoretical guarantees are often studied in normal-form games (Brown, 1951; McMahan et al., 2003) where best-responses can be solved exactly and efficiently. This is, however, in stark contrast to real-world games (Czarnecki et al., 2020) — such games are often temporal in nature, yielding exponentially large policy spaces where best-responses can only be approximated with computationally intensive methods (e.g. deep RL). This has two implications. First, one cannot efficiently tell apart good-responses from best-responses. As a result, approximate best-response procedures are often truncated prematurely, according to hand-crafted schedules (Lanctot et al., 2017). Second, real-world games often afford transitive skill dimensions where the most skilled policy prevails. In this setting, tabula rasa learning in the presence of skillful opponents quickly becomes wasteful and challenging, rendering population learning intractable beyond a few iterations.

This approach is in stark contrast to highly efficient and versatile human learning. Mastering diverse policies in a game often facilitates incremental strategic innovation and learning about new strategies does not stop us from revisiting and improving upon old ones (Caruana, 1997; Krakauer et al., 2006). In this work, we make progress towards endowing artificial agents with similar capacity by extending efficient population learning to real-world games. Specifically, we propose NeuPL, an efficient population learning framework that learns and represents diverse policies in symmetric zero-sum

games within a single conditional network via self-play (Section 1.2). Theoretically, we show that NeuPL converges to a sequence of N-step best-responses under certain conditions (Section 1.4). Empirically, we illustrate the generality of NeuPL by replicating known effects of population learning algorithms on the classical domain of rock-paper-scissors as well as its partially-observed, spatiotemporal counterpart running-with-scissors (Vezhnevets et al., 2020) (Section 2.1). Most interestingly, we show that NeuPL by construction offers skill transfers across policies, discovering best responses to strong opponents that would have been inaccessible to comparable baselines (Section 2.2). Finally, we show the appeal of NeuPL in the skill-based challenge domain of MuJoCo Football (Liu et al., 2019) where players must integrate low-level actions in order to coordinate as a team. In this transitive game-of-skills, NeuPL succinctly represents a short sequence of best-responses, as opposed to an ever-growing population of good-responses if population learning were applied naively (Section 2.4).

# 1 METHODS

Our method is designed with two desiderata in mind. First, at convergence, the resulting population of policies should represent a sequence of iterative N-step best-responses under reasonable conditions. Second, skill transfer can occur across policies throughout training. In this section, we first define the problem setting of interests as well as necessary terminologies. We then describe NeuPL, our main conceptual algorithm as well as its theoretical properties. To make it concrete, we further consider deep RL specifically and offer two practical implementations of NeuPL in real-world games.

# 1.1 PRELIMINARIES

Approximate Best-Response (ABR) in Stochastic Games We consider a symmetric zero-sum Stochastic Game (Shapley, 1953) defined by  $(S, \mathcal{O}, \mathcal{X}, \mathcal{A}, \mathcal{P}, \mathcal{R}, p_0)$  with  $S$  the state space,  $\mathcal{O}$  the observation space and  $\mathcal{X}: S \to \mathcal{O} \times \mathcal{O}$  the observation function defining the (partial) views of the state for both players. Given joint actions  $(a_t, a_t') \in \mathcal{A} \times \mathcal{A}$ , the state follows the transition distribution  $\mathcal{P}: S \times \mathcal{A} \times \mathcal{A} \to \operatorname*{Pr}(S)$ . The reward function  $\mathcal{R}: S \to \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}$  defines the rewards for both players in state  $s_t$ , denoted  $\mathcal{R}(s_t) = (r_t, -r_t)$ . The initial state of the environment follows the distribution  $p_0$ . In a given state  $s_t$ , players act according to policies  $(\pi(\cdot | o_{\leq t}), \pi'(\cdot | o_{\leq t}'))$ . Player  $\pi$  achieves an expected return of  $J(\pi, \pi') = \mathbb{E}_{\pi, \pi'} [\sum_t r_t]$  against  $\pi'$ . Policy  $\pi^*$  is a best response to  $\pi'$  if  $\forall \pi, J(\pi^*, \pi') \geq J(\pi, \pi')$ . We define  $\hat{\pi} \gets \mathrm{ABR}(\pi, \pi')$  with  $J(\hat{\pi}, \pi') \geq J(\pi, \pi')$ . In other words, an ABR procedure yields a policy  $\hat{\pi}$  that does no worse than  $\pi$ , in the presence of an opponent  $\pi'$ .

Meta-strategies in Population Learning Given a symmetric zero-sum game and a set of  $N$  policies  $\Pi \coloneqq \{\pi_i\}_{i = 1}^N$ , we define a normal-form meta-game where players'  $i$ -th action corresponds to executing policy  $\pi_{i}$  for one episode. A meta-strategy  $\sigma$  thus defines a probability assignment, or an action profile, over  $\Pi$ . Within  $\Pi$ , we define  $\mathcal{U} \in \mathbb{R}^{N\times N} \leftarrow \mathrm{EVAL}(\Pi)$  to be the expected payoffs between pure strategies of this meta-game or equivalently,  $\mathcal{U}_{ij} \coloneqq J(\pi_i,\pi_j)$  in the underlying game. We further extend the ABR procedure of the underlying game to mixture policies represented by  $\sigma$ , such that  $\hat{\pi} \gets \mathrm{ABR}(\pi ,\sigma ,\Pi)$  with  $\mathbb{E}_{\pi^{\prime}\sim P(\sigma)}[J(\hat{\pi},\pi^{\prime})]\geq \mathbb{E}_{\pi^{\prime}\sim P(\sigma)}[J(\pi ,\pi^{\prime})]$ . Finally, we define  $f:\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}\to \mathbb{R}^N$  to be a meta-game solver with  $\sigma \gets f(\mathcal{U})$  and  $\mathcal{F}:\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}\rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{N\times N}$  a meta-graph solver with  $\Sigma \gets \mathcal{F}(\mathcal{U})$ . The former formulation is designed for iterative optimization of approximate best-responses as in Lanctot et al. (2017) whereas the latter is motivated by concurrent optimization over a set of population-level objectives as in Garnelo et al. (2021). In particular,  $\Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{N\times N} \coloneqq \{\sigma_i\}_{i = 1}^N$  defines  $N$  population-level objectives, with  $\pi_{i}$  optimized against the mixture policy represented by  $\sigma_{i}$  and  $\Pi$ . As such,  $\Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{N\times N}$  corresponds to an adjacency matrix of an interaction graph. Appendix A.1 illustrates several structured population learning objectives defined by  $\Sigma$  and equivalently, by their interaction graphs.

# 1.2 NEURAL POPULATION LEARNING

We now present NeuPL and contrast it with Policy-Space Response Oracles (PSRO, Lanctot et al. (2017)) which is similarly focused on population learning with approximate best-responses by RL. It's worth noting that NeuPL implements a more general class of population learning algorithms than

PSRO. In particular, NeuPL supports static meta-graph solvers  $\mathcal{F}$  with a constant number of policies (e.g. Section 2.1).

Algorithm 1 Neural Population Learning (Ours)  
1:  $\mathcal{F}:\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}\to \mathbb{R}^{N\times N}$ $\triangleright$  Meta-graph solver.   
2:  $\Pi_{\theta}(\cdot |s,\sigma)$  Conditional neural population net.   
3:  $\Sigma \coloneqq \{\sigma_i\}_{i = 1}^N$ $\triangleright$  Initial interaction graph.   
4: while true do   
5:  $\Pi_{\theta}^{\Sigma}\gets \{\Pi_{\theta}(\cdot |s,\sigma_{i})\}_{i = 1}^{N}$ $\triangleright$  Neural population.   
6: for  $\sigma_{i}\in \mathrm{UNIQUE}(\Sigma)$  do   
7:  $\Pi_{\theta}^{\sigma_i}\gets \Pi_\theta (\cdot |s,\sigma_i)$    
8:  $\Pi_{\theta}^{\sigma_i}\gets \mathrm{ABR}(\Pi_{\theta}^{\sigma_i},\sigma_i,\Pi_{\theta}^{\Sigma})$ $\triangleright$  Self-play.   
9:  $\mathcal{U}\leftarrow \mathrm{EVAL}(\Pi_{\theta}^{\Sigma})$ $\triangleright$  (Optional) if  $\mathcal{F}$  adaptive.   
10:  $\Sigma \gets \mathcal{F}(\mathcal{U})$ $\triangleright$  (Optional) if  $\mathcal{F}$  adaptive.   
11: return  $\Pi_{\theta},\Sigma$

Algorithm 2 PSRO (Lanctot et al., 2017)  
1:  $f: \mathbb{R}^{M \times M} \to \mathbb{R}^{M}$  ▷ Meta-game solver.  
2:  $\Pi := \{\pi_0\}$  ▷ Initial policy population.  
3:  $\sigma \gets \mathrm{UNIF}(\Pi)$  ▷ Initial meta-strategy.  
4:  
5: for  $i \in [[N]]$  do ▷ N-step ABR.  
6: Initialize  $\pi_{\theta_i}$ .  
7:  $\pi_{\theta_i} \gets \mathrm{ABR}(\pi_{\theta_i}, \sigma, \Pi)$   
8:  $\Pi \gets \Pi \cup \{\pi_{\theta_i}\}$   
9:  $\mathcal{U} \gets \mathrm{EVAL}(\Pi)$  ▷ Exp. payoffs.  
10:  $\sigma \gets f(\mathcal{U})$   
11: return  $\Pi$

Comparing the two algorithms, NeuPL deviates from PSRO in two important ways. First, NeuPL suggests concurrent and continued training of all unique policies such that no good-response features in the population prematurely due to early truncation. Second, NeuPL represents an entire population of policies via a shared conditional network  $\Pi_{\theta}(\cdot |s,\sigma)$  with each policy  $\Pi_{\theta}(\cdot |s,\sigma_i)$  conditioned on and optimised against its opponent's meta-game strategy  $\sigma_{i}$ , enabling skill-transfers across policies. This representation also makes NeuPL general, as it delegates the choice of effective population sizes  $|\mathrm{UNIQUE}(\Sigma)|\leq |\Sigma | = N$  to the meta-graph solver  $\mathcal{F}$  as  $\sigma_{i} = \sigma_{j}\Rightarrow \Pi_{\theta}(\cdot |s,\sigma_{i})\equiv \Pi_{\theta}(\cdot |s,\sigma_{j})$  (cf. examples in Section 2.1).

N-step Best-Responses via Lower-Triangular Interaction Graphs A popular class of population learning algorithms aims for convergence to a sequence of iterative best-responses where each policy  $\pi_{i}$  seeks to best-respond to an opponent meta-game strategy  $\sigma_{i}$  with support over a subset of the policy population  $\Pi_{< i} = \{\pi_j\}_{j < i}$ . In NeuPL, this class of algorithms are implemented with meta-graph solvers that return lower-triangular adjacency matrices  $\Sigma$  with  $\Sigma_{i\leq j} = 0$ . Under this constraint,  $\sigma_0$  becomes a zero vector, implying that  $\Pi_{\theta}(\cdot |s,\sigma_0)$  does not seek to best-respond to any policies. Similar to the role of initial policies  $\{\pi_0\}$  in PSRO (Algorithm 2),  $\Pi_{\theta}(\cdot |s,\sigma_0)$  serves as the sink policy for the sequence of N-step best-responses. In practice, any fixed policy can be used and we typically use a random or zero policy depending on the underlying game.

One prominent example is PSRO-NASH, where  $\pi_i$  is optimized to best-respond to the Nash mixture policy over  $\Pi_{<i}$ . This particular meta-game solver is implemented in Algorithm 3.

Algorithm 3 A meta-graph solver implementing PSRO-NASH.  
1: function  $\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{PSRO - N}}(\mathcal{U})$ $\triangleright \mathcal{U}\in \mathbb{R}^{N\times N}$  the empirical payoff matrix.   
2: Initialize meta-game strategies  $\Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{N\times N}$  with zeros.   
3: for  $i\in \{1,\dots ,N - 1\}$  do   
4:  $\Sigma_{i + 1,1:i}\gets \mathrm{SOLVE - NASH}(\mathcal{U}_{1:i,1:i})$  LP Nash solver, see Shoham & Leyton-Brown (2008).   
5: return  $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$

# 1.3 NEURAL POPULATION LEARNING BY RL

We now define the discounted return maximized by  $\Pi_{\theta}(\cdot |o_{\leq t},\sigma_i)$  in Equation 1. We denote  $P(\sigma_i)$  as the probability distribution over policy  $i$  's opponent identities  $\sigma_j\in \{\sigma_1,\dots ,\sigma_N\}$ . Intuitively, each policy is maximizing its expected returns in the underlying game under a double expectation: the first is taken over its opponent distribution, with  $\sigma_{j}\sim P(\sigma_{i})$  and the second taken under the game dynamics partly defined by the pair of policies  $(\Pi_{\theta}(\cdot |o_{\leq t},\sigma_i),\Pi_{\theta}(\cdot |o_{\leq t}'',\sigma_j))$

$$
J _ {\sigma_ {i}} = \underset {\sigma_ {j} \sim P (\sigma_ {i})} {\mathbb {E}} \left[ \underset {a \sim \Pi_ {\theta} (\cdot | o _ {\leq t}, \sigma_ {i}), a ^ {\prime} \sim \Pi_ {\theta} (\cdot | o _ {\leq t} ^ {\prime}, \sigma_ {j})} {\mathbb {E}} \left[ \sum_ {t} r _ {t} \gamma^ {t} \right] \right] \tag {1}
$$

To optimize  $\Pi_{\theta}^{\Sigma}$  by RL, we jointly train an opponent-conditioned action-value $^4$  function, approximating the expected return of choosing an action  $a_t$  given an observation history  $o_{\leq t}$ , following  $\Pi_{\theta}(\cdot | o_{\leq t}, \sigma_i)$  thereafter in the presence of  $\Pi_{\theta}(\cdot | o_{\leq t}', \sigma_j)$ , denoted by  $Q(o_{\leq t}, a_t, \sigma_i, \sigma_j) = \mathbb{E}_{\sigma_i, \sigma_j} \left[ \sum_{\tau = t}^{t + T} \gamma^{\tau - t} r_{\tau} | o_{\leq t}, a_t \right]$  with  $\gamma$  the discount factor. In the case of ABR by deep RL, we could additionally approximate the expected payoffs matrix  $\mathcal{U}$  by learning a payoff estimator  $\phi_{\omega}(\sigma_i, \sigma_j)$  minimizing the loss  $\mathcal{L}_{ij} = \mathbb{E}_{o \sim \mathcal{D}} \left[ (\phi_{\omega}(\sigma_i, \sigma_j) - \mathbb{E}_{a \sim \Pi_{\theta}(\cdot | o, \sigma_i)} [Q_{\theta}(o, a, \sigma_i, \sigma_j)])^2 \right]$  where the expectation is taken over the state visitation distribution  $\mathcal{D}$  defined by the pair of policies and the environment dynamics  $\mathcal{P}$ . In other words,  $\phi_{\omega}(\sigma_i, \sigma_j)$  approximates the expected return of  $\Pi_{\theta}(\cdot | o_{\leq}, \sigma_i)$  playing against  $\Pi_{\theta}(\cdot | o_{\leq}', \sigma_j)$ . By connecting payoff matrix  $\mathcal{U}$  to the learned  $Q$  function, we can evaluate  $\mathcal{U}$  efficiently, without explicitly evaluating all policies at each iteration.

Finally, we propose Algorithm 4 in the setting where the meta-graph solver  $\Sigma^{\mathrm{const}}\gets \mathcal{F}(\mathcal{U}),\forall \mathcal{U}$  is a constant function and extends it to Algorithm 5 where the meta-graph solver is adaptive in  $\mathcal{U}$ . For instance, population learning algorithms such as Fictitious Play (Brown, 1951) implement static interaction graphs while algorithms such as PSRO-NASH (Lanctot et al., 2017) rely on adaptive meta-graph solvers.

# 1.4 CONVERGENCE TO N-STEP BEST-RESPONSES VIA NEUPL

Under certain assumptions on the best respond operator, interaction graph, and meta-graph solver we can construct proofs that NeuPL converges to an  $N$ -step best response. We introduce the term grounded (Section C) to refer to interaction graphs and meta-graph solvers that have a structure that imposes convergence to a unique set of policies. Certain interaction graphs are grounded, in particular, lower-triangular graphs are one such class which describe an  $N$ -step best response. In addition, certain meta-graph solvers are grounded, in particular, ones that operate on the sub-payoff and output a lower-triangular interaction graph,  $\mathcal{F}: \mathcal{U}_{<i, <i} \to \Sigma_{i, <i}$ . The lower-triangular maximum entropy Nash equilibrium (MENE) is one such grounded meta-graph solver. Therefore with sufficiently large  $N$  NeuPL will converge to a normal-form Nash equilibrium. See Section C for the full definitions, theorems and proofs.

# 2 EXPERIMENTS

In this section, we validate different contributions of NeuPL across several domains of varying nature. First, we verify the generality of NeuPL from two aspects: a) NeuPL recovers expected results of existing population learning algorithms (Brown, 1951; Heinrich et al., 2015; Lanctot et al., 2017) on the classical game of rock-paper-scissors where we can visualize the learned policy population over time and; b) NeuPL generalises to the spatiotemporal, partially observed strategy game of running-with-scissors (Vezhnevets et al., 2020), where players must infer opponent behaviours through tactical and skillful interactions. Second, we show that NeuPL induces skill transfer across policies, enabling the discovery of exploiter policies to strong opponents that would have been out-of-reach otherwise. This property translates to improved efficiency and performance compared to PSRO-NASH baselines, even under favorable conditions. Lastly, we show that NeuPL scales to the large-scale game-of-skill of MuJoCo Football (Liu et al., 2019) where a concise sequence of best-responses are learned.

In all experiments, we use Maximum A Posterior Optimization (MPO, Abdelmaleki et al. (2018)) as the underlying RL algorithm, though any alternative can be used instead. Further details of our experimental setup are described in Appendix B.2.

# 2.1 IS NEURAL POPULATION LEARNING GENERAL?

Static Interaction Graphs Figure 1 illustrates the effect of NEUPL-RL-STATIC implementing three population learning algorithms in the purely cyclical domain of rock-paper-scissors. Figure 1 (Left) shows that learning from self-play leads to the policy transitioning through the strategy space indefinitely. This is a well-known result: an agent learning by self-play fails to converge in a purely cyclical game (Balduzzi et al., 2019). By contrast, Figure 1 (Middle) shows the effect of a specialized interaction graph. This graph explicitly encourages the discovery of one strategic cycle (formed by the first three nodes), as well as a final node that seeks to beat the others equally. As a result,

we obtain a population of strategies implementing the pure strategies of the game as well as a mixture strategy<sup>5</sup>. The design of such specific interaction graphs is not always possible as it requires domain knowledge and is only feasible in the simplest games. Figure 1 (Right) illustrates the general population learning algorithm of Fictitious Play (Brown, 1951; Heinrich et al., 2015) where players at each iteration optimize against their "average" previous players. As the sink policy of the N-step best-response sequence, the first strategy could execute any policy and we initialize it to an exploitable policy heavily biased towards playing rock<sup>6</sup>. We observe that the resulting population, captured by  $\Pi_{\theta}(a|o_{\leq},\sigma)$ , learns to execute 6 different strategies, with the first being "rock", followed by a second learning to play pure "paper" to exploit the first and subsequent strategies gravitating towards the Nash equilibrium that cannot be exploited in this game.

Adaptive Interaction Graphs Figure 2 explores the effect of NEUPL-RL-ADAPTIVE implementing  $\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{PSRO - N}}$  in rock-paper-scissors. We make the following observations. First, the first three strategies form a strategic cycle and converge to the pure strategies, while the last strategy optimizes against a mixture of the pure strategies, as expected of PSRO-NASH. We note that as in Figure 1 (Strategic Cycle), the last strategy needs not converge to a Nash strategy. Second, the number of distinct strategies represented by the neural population grows dynamically (comparing  $\Sigma$  at epoch 0 and 71) — a distinct training objective for strategy  $i + 1$  is introduced if and only if  $\Pi_{\theta}(\cdot |o_{\leq},\sigma_i)$  successfully beats the Nash mixture strategy over  $\Pi_{\theta}^{\Sigma < i}$ . Unlike Lanctot et al. (2017), the effective size of the population is driven by the underlying meta-game solver, rather than a handcrafted schedule.

This is particularly appealing in real-world games, where we cannot efficiently determine if a policy has converged to a best-response. The size of the neural population limits the maximum number of strategies represented and optimized concurrently — a size of  $N$  does not imply that the population would optimize  $N$  distinct objectives at the start, nor does it enforce the number of distinct policies to reach  $N$  at convergence. The number of distinct strategies represented by a neural population is primarily governed by the dynamics of the underlying game, the generalisation capacity of the neural network, the effectiveness of the RL algorithm and the meta-game solver  $\mathcal{F}$ . We later recall this property in running-with-scissors and in MuJoCo Football, where the underlying game affords varying degrees of strategic complexities.

Stochastic Games The rich strategic domain of running-with-scissors (Vezhnevets et al., 2020) extends the game of rock-paper-scissors to the spatiotemporal and partially observable setting. Using first-person partial observations of the game (a small window in front of the agent), each player collects resources representing "rock", "paper" and "scissors" so as to counter its opponent's unobserved inventory. At the end of an episode or when players confront each other through "tagging", players compare their inventories and receive rewards according to the rock-paper-scissors payoff table. To do well, an agent must learn to infer its opponent's behaviours from partial observation history  $o_{\leq t}$ . For instance, if "rock"s are missing, then the opponent may be collecting them; if the opponent is seen running past a "scissors", then it may not be interested in "scissors". We describe the environment in details in Appendix B.1. We show in Figure 3 that NeuPL with an adaptive meta-graph solver  $\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{PSRO - N}}$  results in a population of sophisticated policies. As before, we set the first policy (sink policy) to be heavily exploitable and biased towards picking up "rock"s. Early in training, we note that the first three policies of the neural population implement the pure-resource policies of "rock", "paper" and "scissors" respectively, as evidenced by their relative payoffs. In contrast to rock-paper-scissors, the mixture of pure-resource policies is exploitable in the sequential setting, where the player can observe its opponent before implementing a counter strategy. Indeed, policy  $\Pi_{\theta}(\cdot |o_{\leq},\sigma_4)$  employs the tactic of "observe-and-exploit", successfully beating the mixture policies at epoch 680. Following  $\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{PSRO - N}}$ ,  $\Pi_{\theta}(\cdot |o_{\leq},\sigma_5)$  updates its objective to focus solely on this newfound Nash equilibrium over  $\Pi_{\theta}^{\Sigma < 5}$ , eventually developing a deceptive counter strategy. Example episodes between all 8 policies are visualized on the project website.

We verify quantitatively that NeuPL implementing  $\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{PSRO - N}}$  similarly induces a policy population that becomes robust to adversarial exploits, as expected of PSRO-NASH (Lanctot et al., 2017). We compare independent policy populations and measure their Relative Population Performance (RPP, Appendix A.1). Intuitively, a negative RPP between populations  $(\mathfrak{B},\mathfrak{D})$  implies that there exists a mixture policy in  $\mathfrak{D}$  that exploits all mixture policies over  $\mathfrak{B}$ . Figure 4 (Left) shows this metric measured at different stages of learning across 4 independent NeuPL experiments with different maximum population sizes. First, we observe that a neural population of maximum size two is easily exploited by all other populations and increasingly so as training progresses. This is expected, as the population converges to playing the two pure-resource policies ("rock" and "paper"). A larger population of size four is more robust, covering the single resource policies in addition to the policy that "observe-and-exploit". This population however becomes exploitable to the larger neural populations eventually as they discover exploiters that intentionally "mislead" its opponents. Finally, we note that a neural population of size greater than eight has limited impact on learning, both in terms

of additional robustness benefits by observing that relative population performance tends towards zero and their comparable rate of improvement against smaller populations (shown in blue and orange). In fact, Figure 4 (Right) shows that the effective population size  $|\mathrm{UNIQUE}(\Sigma)|$  represented by each neural population plateaus at 12, regardless of the specified maximum capacities of the neural populations. We hypothesise that this is due to the increased difficulty in discovering reliable exploiter policies in this domain. As noted in Section 1.2,  $\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{PSRO - N}}$  forms an efficient curriculum where new objectives are introduced when the population discovers new meta-strategies worth exploiting.

# 2.2 DOES NEUPL ENABLE SKILL TRANSFER ACROSS POLICIES?

When coupled with deep RL, population learning algorithms such as Fictitious Self-Play and PSRO are often implemented as learning an approximate best response at each iteration from scratch (Heinrich et al., 2015; Lanctot et al., 2017; Mcaleer et al., 2020). In comparison, a NeuPL population represents different policies with a shared understanding of the game through parameter sharing. Figure 5 compares the two approaches and illustrates the important role of skill transfer offered by NeuPL. Specifically, we verify that the shared representation learned by training against fewer, weaker policies early in training, facilitates the learning of exploiters to stronger, previously unseen opponents. To verify this statement, a set of randomly initialized MPO agents with partially transferred parameters from different epochs shown in Figure 3 are optimized against the opponent mixtures defined by  $\Pi_{\theta^*}^{\Sigma^*}$ , where  $\theta^*$  and  $\Sigma^* = \mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{PSRO - N}}(\mathcal{U}^*)$  are obtained at epoch 1,200 from the same NeuPL experiment. In other words, the objective for each MPO agent is to perform well against a fixed Nash mixture over pre-trained policies  $\{\Pi_{\theta^*}(a|o_{\le},\sigma_k^*)\}_{k = 1}^n$ , with a specific  $n$ . Figure 5 shows the learning progressions of the MPO agents for three objectives,  $n\in \{2,4,7\}$ , with partially transferred parameters taken at epoch 0 (red) upto 1,000 (green).

Against an easily exploitable opponent mixture (Nash distribution over the first two pure policies), an agent with randomly initialized parameters (red) remains capable of learning an effective best response, albeit at a slower pace than agents partially initialized with transferred network parameters

This difference becomes much more apparent against competent opponent mixtures that executes sophisticated policies (Nash distributions over the first 4 and 7 policies) where a randomly initialized agent fails to discover effective exploits from random initialization. By contrast, agents starting with partially transferred network parameters successfully discovered exploits, leveraging effective representation of the environment dynamics and crucially, of diverse opponents. Learning through NeuPL, this shared representation capacity enables the discovery of novel policies that are inaccessible to a randomly initialized agent. For a NeuPL population, learning incremental best responses becomes easier, not harder, as the agent gains better understanding of the game. This property is particularly attractive in real-world games where representation learning is often a challenge by itself (Jaderberg et al., 2019; Vinyals et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2021).

# 2.3 DOES NEUPL OUTPERFORM COMPARABLE BASELINE?

![](images/dcee791b4843c4779a5f42904ada4b261c886b5d011a9f99648bba7d2e7afa03.jpg)  
Figure 6: Relative Population Performance between a NeuPL population and policy populations obtained in PSRO baselines. Each PSRO variant is repeated with 3 trials, shown in shades.

We compare a NeuPL population implementing  $\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{PSRO - N}}$  to four baselines implementing variants of PSRO. While PSRO does not prescribe a schedule for generating novel learning objectives, we investigate PSRO baselines with iteration length of 100k and 200k gradient steps respectively. Further, we consider the effect of continued training across iterations, by learning iterative best responses starting from the policy obtained at the end of the preceding iteration, instead of random initialization. We refer to this continued variant as PSRO-C. All PSRO populations are initialized with the same sink policy used in the NeuPL population. Figure 6 illustrates the quantitative benefits of NeuPL, measuring the Relative Population Performance between a NeuPL population of maximum population size of 8 against the final population of 8 policies obtained via PSRO after 7 iterations. A positive RPP value indicates that the NeuPL population beats the population of PSRO policies while a negative value indicates the opposite. The vertical dashed lines indicate that both the NeuPL population and the PSRO population have cumulatively undergone identical amount of training to allow for fair comparison. In purple, we show the effective population size of the NeuPL population which has been shown previously in Figure 4. We make the following observations: i) with a population size of 8, the NeuPL population successfully exploits PSRO baselines representing an equal number of policies, even when the latter received more training per iteration; ii) the increase in RPP coincides with an increase in the effective population size, from 5 to 8, reaching the maximum number of distinct policies that this NeuPL population can represent; iii) the amount of training each PSRO generation received has limited impact on the robustness of policy populations at convergence. This corroborates our observations of PSRO in Figure 5, where the agent (in red) failed to exploit strong opponents despite continued training. Interestingly, PSRO-C proves equally exploitable by the NeuPL population. We hypothesize that this is because at each iteration, the learned policy overfits to a specific opponent, rather than developing a versatile representation supporting diverse strategies. We show the payoff matrices for the PSRO baselines across three seeds in Appendix B.3.

# 2.4 DOES NEUPL SCALE TO COMPLEX GAME-OF-SKILLS?

In contrast to domains that primarily focus on strategic complexity, MuJoCo Football domain (Liu et al., 2019) challenges agents to integrate high-frequency, continuous actions to perform long-horizon team coordination. Figure 7 shows the learning progression of NeuPL implementing  $\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{PSRO - N}}$  in

![](images/2312769c942a899bcb9de549801ec60b88b720ab1bbe846aafa330d1d1f596d9.jpg)  
Figure 7: NeuPL in 2-vs-2 MuJoCo Football implementing  $\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{PSRO - N}}$ , with a static sink policy. The red/blue/white traces correspond to the trajectories of red/blue players and the ball respectively. The circles highlight the latest position of different entities.

this domain, starting with a sink policy that exerts zero torque on all actuators. Qualitatively, we observe that  $\Pi_{\theta}(\cdot |o_{\leq},\sigma_2)$  optimally exploits the sink policy by making rapid, long-range shots from a distance (Figure 7 (Middle)). This policy is in turn countered by  $\Pi_{\theta}(\cdot |o_{<},\sigma_3)$ , which learned to intercept shots and coordinate as a team to score. Most impressively, the off-ball blue player blocked off red defenders, creating scoring opportunities for its teammate (Figure 7 (Right)).

Besides scaling up to this complex domain and developing a sequence of interesting and coordinated behaviours, NeuPL further revealed the underlying transitive structure of this domain, with the meta-graph solver  $\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{PSRO - N}}$  concentrating on the lower-diagonal elements. This implies policy  $i$  dominates  $\Pi_{< i}$  and this regime effectively reduces to that of self-play, an effective strategy in purely transitive games (Balduzzi et al., 2019). For consistency, we used similar encoder, memory network architectures as in Liu et al. (2019) while keeping the RL algorithm the same with the rest of our experiments. Additional videos showing the behaviours of individual policies are available on the project website.

# 3 RELATED WORK

Our work shares similar motivation as multi-task learning where a single agent learns to solve a range of related tasks (Caruana, 1997), either simultaneously, or in a continual setting (French, 1999; Barreto et al., 2020). In this work, we adopted similar techniques as in Schaul et al. (2015), but arguably in a more natural setting where tasks are generated by the task solvers themselves, calling for transfer between tasks, but also, over time. From a population learning perspective, our work targets the same setting as Lanctot et al. (2017), but embeds approximate best-responses with a focus on representational and computational efficiencies. Concurrent optimisation of several population-level objectives was featured in Garnelo et al. (2021), too, but in a setting where a fixed number of policies are trained. Vadori et al. (2020) attempted at representing policies of different types via a shared network, though types are pre-defined with domain-specific prior-knowledge.

# 4 CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK

We proposed a principled population learning framework that optimizes a single conditional model to efficiently learn and represent a range of diverse policies in real-world games. Importantly, our work reduces the computational costs of population learning to that of self-play, making population learning on real-world games accessible to the broader research community. In this work, we restricted ourselves to simple network architecture and multi-task learning techniques but exploring suitable inductive biases in the context of structured population learning could be a productive direction. From a game theory perspective, generalizing NeuPL beyond the symmetric zero-sum setting (Muller et al., 2020; Marris et al., 2021) remain interesting future works. Finally, scaling up our method to very large-scale, strategically rich domains such as StarCraft could be an exciting next step.
